title: Runtime ops tradeoffs & buy-vs-build talking kit
content:
Goal:
Provide SEs, SDRs and PMs a compact, scenario-driven kit to discuss self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM) vs Redwood. Focus on concrete operational scenarios, realistic time-to-resolution estimates, and language that resonates with engineering buyers who care about control and cost.

One-sentence positioning to lead with:
If your team values maximum control today but also needs predictable uptime, cost stability, and fast recovery from infra regressions, Redwood is the pragmatic middle path: keep experimentation flexible, outsource the long tail of runtime ops.

Top three buyer profiles and tailored messages:
- Prototype-first ML team (small infra budget): "Run what you want to iterate quickly. When usage grows, avoid hiring an ops team — Redwood can absorb scale pain so your product team doesn’t."
- Platform/Infra team (internal cloud operators): "You want control and observability. Redwood plugs into your VPC and preserves policy controls while giving a hardened runtime, freeing your team to build higher-level primitives."
- Cost-sensitive enterprise (central finance scrutiny): "We make unit economics auditable and reduce surprise incidents that force expensive emergency work or rush-hire contractors."

Scenario vignettes (concrete, story-based rebuttals):
1) The Kernel Surprise
   Situation: Your infra team runs TensorRT-LLM optimized instances. A CUDA driver update produces a subtle numeric drift that changes model ranking in production.
   Impact: Silent quality regression, degraded user experience for several hours to days while root cause is chased.
   How Redwood helps: we maintain compatibility layers, automated regression checks on rollout, and instant fallback to a validated variant. Time-to-detect and rollback measured in minutes, not days.

2) The Burst Event
   Situation: Holiday promotion spikes traffic with longer prompt chains; autoscaler misconfigures token-based demand leading to queueing and consistent p99 spikes.
   Impact: Customer SLAs hit, hotfixes, and emergency capacity procurement.
   How Redwood helps: workload-aware autoscaling tuned to token distribution, burst offload to dedicated pools, and routing policies to degrade gracefully (e.g., shorter-variant fallback).

3) The Multi-model Matrix
   Situation: Multiple teams run different quantization profiles and frequent model swaps; a single GPU fleet must support heterogeneous memory/sequence patterns.
   Impact: Inefficient packing, high interruption rates, and KV-cache invalidation.
   How Redwood helps: model-aware packing, prefix caching policies, and per-route cost/latency attribution so teams stop arguing about shared pool priorities.

Practical objections and short evidence-led counters:
- "We can just save money with on-prem GPUs."
  Evidence-led counter: initial hardware TCO ignores year-over-year ops tax. We recommend asking for the last 12 months of incidents related to runtime upgrades, and multiplying nominal GPU savings by 2x to account for recurring ops/engineering time.

- "We need TensorRT for peak efficiency."
  Counter: tensorRT is excellent for narrow, stable workloads. If your roadmap includes model churn, variable prompt lengths, or multi-tenancy, the efficiency wins are frequently negated by the engineering effort to sustain that stack. Redwood supports TensorRT-backed variants while managing upgrades and fallbacks.

- "We’ll keep everything in a VPC — that solves control concerns."
  Counter: VPCs solve networking/isolation but not the operational burden of kernel upgrades, caching behavior, long-tail latency, or cost attribution. Redwood Private keeps data within your network while providing the operational primitives.

Checklist: what the customer must build if they go self-hosted (quick bullets):
- CI for driver/TensorRT upgrades with numerical-diff tests per model
- Token-aware autoscaler and test harness for burst scenarios
- Per-model quantization validation suite and rollback scripts
- Sharding & KV-cache warming strategy for low-cold-start latency
- Observability for token-level trails (p50/p95/p99/p999), cache hit metrics, and route cost breakdowns
- Incident runbooks and postmortem templates specifically for model-regression incidents

Suggested SE playbook for discovery calls (questions to ask):
- How often do you change models or tokenization layers? (weekly, monthly, quarterly)
- What are your real p99 and p999 targets, not p95?
- Describe your peak prompt length and how often long prompts appear (percentile).
- Which internal SLAs force human intervention on an incident?

Two short scripts:
- For skeptical infra lead: "We don’t want to replace your control plane. Think of Redwood as an operationally hardened runtime you can plug into — keep your policies, offload the heartache of kernel upgrades and tail latency hunting."
- For engineering manager: "If you want to ship features and not spend cycles on runtime sledding, Redwood reduces your incident load and gives measurable unit economics so you can plan hires rationally."

Metrics to gather during POC (SEs should ask customers to run these):
- Realized tokens/sec vs provisioned GPUs during synthetic bursts
- p99/p999 latency under mixed-length workloads
- Percent of requests served from prefix/KV cache vs cold starts
- Frequency and duration of degraded-mode incidents during an upgrade window

Migration playbook (recommended, low friction):
- Week 0: baseline — capture request mix, token-length distribution, p99 baseline from their stack.
- Week 1: pilot — route 5-10% of production traffic to Redwood Dedicated; measure variant behavior and rollback time.
- Week 3: canary — ramp to 25-50% with canary-specific prompts and run regression checks.
- Week 6: hybrid steady-state — keep sensitive endpoints on private/on-prem while sending burst/offload traffic to Redwood.

Open asks for product/benchmarking team:
- Build a short, reproducible benchmark that mimics mixed prompt workloads (session + streaming) and runs in <90 minutes on a customer laptop or small cloud VM.
- Produce two anonymized upgrade regression stories with quantitative impact and ops-hours logged.

Tone guidance for GTM:
Pragmatic and technical. Avoid fearmongering. Acknowledge that prototyping on vLLM/TGI is smart; lead with the long-term engineering cost and offer migration lanes that respect the buyers desire for control.

Appendix: three quick technical differentiators (one-line each)
- vLLM: great for rapid iteration and CPU-friendly experiments; requires bespoke scheduler tuning for high-throughput GPU fleets.
- TGI: nice Transformer ecosystem integration; operationally needs careful format/version management when quantized kernels are used.
- TensorRT-LLM: unmatched throughput in constrained configs; upgrade coupling (CUDA/driver/TensorRT) makes maintenance cycles costly.

End of brief.
